opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think it's one of the more interesting open areas right now. In some ways diffusion models are actually a nice setting for interpretability, because the mathematical framework underneath them is quite clean. At the core, what the network is learning is the score function, the gradient of the log density of the data, at different noise levels. So we have a pretty good understanding of *what* the network is supposed to be computing in principle. The part that's still very much a black box is *how* a particular deep network, a U-Net or a transformer, actually represents and computes that function internally.

So I tend to think about interpretability at a couple of different levels. One is the process level: understanding what happens along the denoising trajectory. There's been a lot of nice work showing that at high noise levels the model is essentially making coarse, global decisions, like layout, composition, the overall semantics, and as you go to lower noise levels it's filling in finer details and textures. That gives you a natural handle for interpretability and also for control, because you can intervene at different points in the trajectory and see what changes.

Then there's the representation level, which is closer to what people do with language models: probing the intermediate activations, looking at attention maps, especially cross-attention in text-to-image models, to see which parts of the prompt influence which parts of the image. People have found that these internal features are surprisingly semantic. You can use them for segmentation or correspondence without any extra training, which suggests the models are learning fairly meaningful structure about the world just from trying to denoise.

And then there's a more theoretical question I find really fascinating, which is about generalization versus memorization. If you solved the denoising objective perfectly on a finite training set, the optimal score function would just reproduce the training data. The fact that these models generate novel samples means the network's inductive biases, the architecture, the optimization, are doing something important. Understanding exactly what those inductive biases are is, to me, a form of interpretability too, and probably one of the deeper scientific questions in the field.

From a practical standpoint, I think it matters a lot. If we want to use these models in science, for designing molecules or materials, or in high-stakes settings, we need to understand when to trust them, why they produce what they produce, and how to steer them reliably. So I'm optimistic. The probabilistic structure gives us more to work with than we have for many other deep learning systems, but there's still a lot of work to do to connect that nice math to what's happening inside the actual networks.

r001.rationale: The response does not say diffusion models are expected to be similar to other deep neural networks in interpretability; it says their probabilistic structure gives more to work with.

r002.rationale: The response is optimistic about interpretability research and describes several promising avenues rather than expressing skepticism.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly I think it's an area where we're still at a very early stage. Diffusion models are a bit of an interesting case, because at one level they're actually quite interpretable. The generative process is very explicit. You start from noise, and you gradually denoise, step by step, and at each step the model is essentially estimating the gradient of the log density of the data, the score function. So from a mathematical perspective, you know exactly what the model is supposed to be computing. That's quite different from, say, a GAN, where the generator is just a black box mapping noise to images and there isn't really a principled story for what the intermediate layers mean.

But of course the thing that actually computes the score is a big neural network, a U-Net or increasingly a transformer, and that part we don't understand much better than we understand any other deep network. So I'd say the interpretability is at the level of the algorithm, not at the level of the parameters.

That said, I think the structure does give you some useful handles. One is the time axis. Because you can look at what the model is doing at high noise levels versus low noise levels, and you see that it tends to commit to coarse, global structure early, things like layout and composition, and then fill in fine detail later. So you can sort of localize what kind of information is being decided at each stage, which is harder to do in a single forward pass model. Another handle is the connection to probability. Because you have access to likelihoods, at least approximately, you can ask fairly principled questions about what the model has learned about the data distribution, where it assigns mass, how it generalizes beyond the training set, things like memorization, which has become a very practical concern.

Where I think the field is lagging is in the more mechanistic style of interpretability that people have been doing on language models, actually looking inside the network, finding features or circuits that correspond to concepts. There's some early work in that direction, on things like the attention maps in text to image models, which turn out to be fairly meaningful and have been used for controlling generation. But it's much less mature than what we see on the language side, and I think that's partly just because the community working on diffusion has been more focused on sample quality and speed.

So my overall view is that it's underexplored, but it's also a case where the math gives you more to work with than usual, and I'd like to see more people take advantage of that structure rather than treating the network as a generic black box.

r001.rationale: The response says the neural network component is no better understood than other deep networks, but also describes diffusion models as interpretable at the algorithm level and as offering useful interpretability handles.

r002.rationale: The response calls interpretability underexplored and less mature, but advocates further research; it does not express skepticism toward interpretability research.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a very interesting research direction. With diffusion models, we have a fairly clear mathematical understanding of the process we’re trying to learn: you add noise to data, and then you learn how to reverse that process. But that doesn’t necessarily mean we understand how the neural network accomplishes each denoising step, or what it has learned about the structure of the data.

One question I find interesting is whether we can connect those two levels of understanding. How does the network use information at different noise levels? When does it establish the overall structure of a sample, and how does it refine the details? Having a mathematical description of the overall procedure gives us a useful starting point, but there’s still a lot to understand about the learned computation.

r001.rationale: The response discusses what is and isn’t understood about diffusion models, but does not say their interpretability is expected to be similar to that of other deep neural network models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a very interesting research direction. With diffusion models, we have a fairly clean mathematical description of the overall process: you add noise to data, and then you learn how to reverse that process. But that doesn’t mean we understand what the neural network has learned or how it makes a particular decision at each step.

One useful perspective is that the network is learning something about the geometry of the data distribution—directions that take a noisy example toward more likely examples. That gives us a starting point for interpretation. But connecting those directions to concepts that humans understand is still challenging.

So I would distinguish understanding the algorithm from understanding the learned model. We can say quite a lot about the former, while there are still many open questions about the latter. And I think studying that gap could help us understand both why these models work so well and when they fail.
